extraction.citation: Olmstead SM (2004). Thirsty colonias: Rate regulation and the provision of water service. Land Economics 80(1):136-150.
extraction.subnational_unit: Cameron, El Paso, Hidalgo and Webb counties (Texas-Mexico border)
extraction.legal_system: common law (United States; Texas Water Code)
extraction.urban_rural: mixed (34% of sample colonias urban, 66% rural)
extraction.service_provider: non-profit water supply corporations (about 75% of sample colonias), municipal systems, county systems and general-law water districts, private for-profit suppliers (about 2%), and colonias with only wells, hauled water or no identified provider
extraction.regulatory_model: Texas water service in colonias: rates of municipal systems are set internally, rates of county systems and districts are regulated by the state environmental commission (TCEQ), while non-profit water supply corporations and for-profit suppliers are not rate-regulated (rates and connection costs can be appealed to TCEQ); providers differ in debt-issuing and taxing authority and in access to low-cost federal and state funds (Rural Development, the Economically Distressed Areas Program); legal service areas (certificates of convenience and necessity); no mandatory universal service; counties may enforce the state's model subdivision rules (MSR) in unincorporated areas since 1989
extraction.population: residents of colonias (low-income, mostly unincorporated border settlements without basic services) in four Texas border counties: 781 colonias with 267,384 residents in 1996
extraction.sample_size: 781 colonias (267,384 residents in 1996; the four counties hold 73% of Texas colonias and 75% of the colonia population); a subset of the available data, merged from the Texas Water Development Board Colonias Database (1992 and 1996) and the Attorney General's Texas Border Database
extraction.effect_estimate: Probability that a colonia had obtained water service by 1996 (probit; mean 0.86 in the sample). Model B: provider subject to price regulation, coefficient -1.1858 (SE 0.4163, p = 0.004), marginal effect -0.2718, i.e. about 27 percentage points lower probability of service; access to Rural Development funding 0.2162 (p = 0.401, not significant); county cited for lax enforcement of the model subdivision rules -7.5722 (p = 0.004), marginal effect -0.6943; median per capita income +0.1410 (p = 0.001); population (ln) +0.3776. Model A (provider type against private for-profit): non-profit corporation -0.3795 (p = 0.535), municipal -1.9433 (p = 0.051), district or county -1.1105 (p = 0.035), wells or unknown -2.3819 (p = 0.007). Urban colonias are about 5.6 points more likely to be served. The author concludes that rate regulation, intended to make service affordable, may reduce coverage among the poor where there is no universal-service mandate, and that pricing flexibility matters more than public infrastructure subsidies.
extraction.covariates: colonia population (1996), median per capita income (1989), urban or rural status, access to Rural Development funding, colonia population as a share of county population, months taken by the county to pass the model subdivision rules, county cited for violations of those rules
extraction.model_type: probit regression (Model A: provider-type indicators; Model B: price regulation and rural-development funding); standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and clustered by infrastructure-project group
extraction.study_design: cross-sectional observational probit analysis of colonias in four Texas border counties (merged agency databases; sample-selection and omitted-variable limits acknowledged by the author)
extraction.risk_of_bias_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
extraction.risk_of_bias_rating: Some concern (appraised 2026-10-14 on the full text against the official JBI Cross Sectional checklist; items 1-8: Unclear (the sample is the colonias with data in both agency databases in four counties, a subset of the available data), Yes (setting and population described, Tables 2 and 3), Unclear (price regulation is coded from the provider type, and for unserved colonias from the most likely provider), Yes (service status 1996 from an agency database), Yes (income, population, urban status, funding access and county enforcement identified), Yes (included as covariates; omitted political variables acknowledged), Unclear (agency-compiled data, no validity check; water quality not measured), Yes (probit with marginal effects, robust clustered standard errors); 5/8 Yes)
extraction.selection_bias: Moderate (four border counties and the colonias present in both databases; a subset of the available data, as the author notes)
extraction.measurement_bias: Moderate (provider type for unserved colonias is the most likely provider; service status from an agency database; water quality not measured)
extraction.confounding: Moderate (income, population, urban status, funding access and county enforcement controlled; political variables omitted, as the author notes)
extraction.reporting_bias: Low to moderate (two models reported; main result tied to the author's stated hypotheses)
extraction.legal_measurement_quality: moderate (price regulation coded from the provider type under the Texas Water Code (Table 2); county enforcement from citations for violations of the model subdivision rules; actual rate levels not measured)
extraction.outcome_measurement_quality: moderate (binary service status in 1996 from the Colonias Database; an upper bound on safe access; water quality not measured)
extraction.table: Tables 2-5 (Table 2 provider characteristics; Table 3 summary statistics; Tables 4 and 5 Models A and B)
extraction.section: Full text (journal article, 15 pages, scanned images read as page images): Introduction; Historical background; Theory; Data description; Econometric analysis; Conclusion
extraction.exact_location: Table 3 (summary statistics, p. 144); Model B (price regulation) in the econometric section

evidence_map.evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a cross-sectional probit analysis of 781 colonias in four Texas border counties (1996) estimating how price regulation of the water provider and other provider characteristics relate to whether a colonia had obtained water service; adjusted, JBI Some concern; read in full text (pages 2-15) 2026-10-14.
evidence_map.institutional_context: Texas colonias: rate regulation of municipal, county and district providers (TCEQ), unregulated non-profit water supply corporations, certificates of convenience and necessity, county enforcement of model subdivision rules, state and federal infrastructure funding programmes
